content: Uterine tachysystole, defined as more than five contractions in a 10-minute period over two consecutive intervals, is a common occurrence during labor, particularly when labor-stimulating agents are used. This condition can compromise fetal oxygenation by disrupting maternal blood flow to the placenta during contractions. Reducing the frequency of uterine contractions may improve placental blood flow and, consequently, fetal oxygenation. The purpose of this review was to assess the use of tocolytic agents to reduce or halt uterine contractions in order to improve the condition of the fetus in utero. This review updates and replaces a previous Cochrane Review on the same topic. The objective of this review was to evaluate the effects of acute tocolysis during labor for uterine tachysystole, suspected fetal distress, or both, on outcomes for the fetus, mother, and neonate. The review included randomized controlled trials (RCTs) that investigated the use of tocolytics in these scenarios. Eight studies involving 734 women were included, conducted primarily in hospital settings in high-income countries (e.g., the USA, Austria, Uruguay), with two studies from middle-income countries (South Africa and Sri Lanka). All hospitals involved had the capacity to perform cesarean sections. The overall risk of bias in the studies was low, except for issues related to blinding. All trials included a selective beta2-adrenergic agonist in at least one treatment arm, though the specific drugs and comparators varied. Limited data were available on maternal outcomes. Key Findings: 1. Selective Beta2-Adrenergic Agonist vs. No Tocolytic Agent (Awaiting Emergency Delivery): Two stillbirths occurred in the no-tocolytic control group. One case involved gross hydrocephalus, and the other occurred after a 55-minute delay for cesarean section. The risk ratio (RR) was 0.23 (95% CI 0.01 to 4.55; low-quality evidence). Abnormal fetal heart rate patterns were less frequent with tocolytic treatment (RR 0.28, 95% CI 0.08 to 0.95; moderate-quality evidence). The effect on the number of neonates with an Apgar score below seven was uncertain (low-quality evidence). 2. Intravenous (IV) Atosiban vs. IV Hexoprenaline (1 Study, 26 Women): One infant in the hexoprenaline group required more than 24 hours in the neonatal intensive care unit (NICU) following a forceps delivery (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.50; low-quality evidence). No fetal or neonatal deaths were reported, and no neonates had Apgar scores below seven. One cesarean delivery occurred in the hexoprenaline group (RR 0.33, 95% CI 0.01 to 7.50; low-quality evidence). One case of abnormal fetal heart rate was reported in the atosiban group (RR 3.00, 95% CI 0.13 to 67.51; very low-quality evidence). 3. IV Fenoterol Bromhydrate vs. Emergency Delivery (1 Study, 390 Women): No data were reported for perinatal death, severe morbidity, or fetal/neonatal mortality. IV fenoterol was associated with a probable increase in the risk of cesarean delivery (RR 1.12, 95% CI 1.04 to 1.22; moderate-quality evidence). Fenoterol may have little or no effect on the risk of Apgar scores below seven (RR 1.28, 95% CI 0.35 to 4.68; low-quality evidence). 4. IV Hexoprenaline vs. No Tocolytic Agent (Awaiting Emergency Delivery, 1 Study, 37 Women): No data were reported for perinatal death or severe morbidity. Two fetal deaths occurred in the no-tocolytic control group (RR 0.23, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.55; low-quality evidence). The rate of cesarean delivery was not reported. Two neonates in the control group had Apgar scores below seven, compared to none in the hexoprenaline group (RR 0.24, 95% CI 0.01 to 4.57; low-quality evidence). 5. Subcutaneous Terbutaline vs. IV Magnesium Sulfate (1 Study, 46 Women): No data were reported for perinatal death, severe morbidity, or fetal/neonatal mortality. The decision for cesarean section was an inclusion criterion, so this outcome could not be assessed. The effect on abnormal fetal heart rate patterns was uncertain (very low-quality evidence). 6. Subcutaneous Terbutaline with Continuation of Oxytocic Infusion vs. Cessation of Oxytocic Infusion Without Tocolytic Agent (1 Study, 28 Women): No data were reported for perinatal death, severe morbidity, or fetal/neonatal mortality. There may be little or no difference in cesarean delivery rates between the terbutaline group (8/15) and the control group (4/13) (RR 1.73, 95% CI 0.68 to 4.45; low-quality evidence). No cases of Apgar scores below seven or abnormal fetal heart rate patterns were reported. 7. Subcutaneous Terbutaline vs. No Tocolytic Agent (Awaiting Emergency Delivery, 1 Study, 20 Women): No data were reported for perinatal death or severe morbidity. No fetal or neonatal deaths occurred. Two neonates in the control group had Apgar scores below seven, compared to none in the terbutaline group (RR 0.17, 95% CI 0.01 to 3.08; low-quality evidence). 8. IV Terbutaline vs. IV Nitroglycerin (1 Study, 110 Women): No data were reported for perinatal death, severe morbidity, or fetal/neonatal mortality. There may be little or no difference in cesarean delivery rates between the terbutaline group (30/57) and the nitroglycerin group (29/53) (RR 0.96, 95% CI 0.68 to 1.36; low-quality evidence). No cases of Apgar scores below seven were reported. Authors' Conclusions: The evidence is insufficient to determine the effects of tocolytics for uterine tachysystole or suspected fetal distress during labor. While some measures of fetal well-being showed improvement with tocolytics, the clinical significance of these findings remains unclear. The sample sizes of the included studies were too small to detect meaningful effects on neonatal morbidity, mortality, or serious adverse outcomes. Most studies were conducted in high-income countries with access to cesarean sections, limiting the generalizability of the findings to lower-resource settings or locations without cesarean availability. Further well-designed and adequately powered RCTs are needed to evaluate clinically relevant maternal and neonatal outcomes.
